analysis.title: US Daily: September Payrolls Preview
key_insights: GS estimates September nonfarm payrolls rose 80k, slightly below consensus of +88k and above the three-month average of +71k. Private payrolls are estimated at +75k versus consensus of +80k.

Arguing for a stronger report: initial jobless claims averaged 204k in the September payroll month, in line with August. The JOLTS layoff rate fell 0.1pp to 1.0% in August, and Challenger announced layoffs fell 2k to 52k in September (SA by GS).
Alternative employment data picked up. The indicators GS tracks averaged +77k in September versus +31k in August, though slightly below the consensus estimate.
Arguing for a weaker report: Labor Day fell on September 7th, which is relatively late. In past Septembers with a Labor Day that late, payroll growth has generally underperformed the recent trend.

August job growth was overstated. Rebounds in local government educational services and leisure and hospitality added a combined 104k. GS expects these not to repeat. It says the gains likely reflected normalization after similar declines over the prior two months, and that large summer swings in these series make them hard to seasonally adjust.

Job availability is mixed. Averaged across JOLTS, Indeed and LinkUp, openings were roughly unchanged in August, and Indeed and LinkUp were stable in September. The Conference Board labor differential fell 2.5pt to +1.7 in September.

Employment components of GS's manufacturing (+1.0pt to 53.2) and services (+1.4pt to 51.4) survey trackers rose in September. GS says survey signals have been less useful and at times misleading post-pandemic, so they have little bearing on its payrolls forecast.

GS forecasts average hourly earnings +0.2% month over month, below consensus of 0.3%, because of negative calendar effects. Its wage tracker has preliminarily risen 3.1% quarter over quarter annualized and 3.5% year over year in Q3.
GS now estimates the unemployment rate edged down to 4.0% from 4.1%, reflecting lower continuing claims. Its earlier forecast was in line with consensus and the prior month at 4.1%.

GS's slack tracker, built from ten measures of labor market slack and scaled to unemployment-rate units, has declined over recent months but stands at 4.6%. GS says this suggests the labor market is somewhat softer than the unemployment rate alone implies.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Slightly below the +88k consensus and above the +71k three-month average. A late Labor Day and a non-repeat of August's education and leisure gains weigh on the estimate.
Street expectation that GS sits slightly below.
GS is also slightly below consensus on the private-sector component.
The GS estimate of +80k sits above this recent trend.
GS cut its forecast by a tenth, citing the decline in continuing claims. It had previously been in line with consensus at 4.1%.
Below consensus because of negative calendar effects.

macro_indicators.reading: 3.1% quarter over quarter annualized, 3.5% year over year
macro_indicators.interpretation: Preliminary reading combining average hourly earnings, the employment cost index, the Atlanta Fed wage tracker, compensation per hour and usual weekly wages.
In line with August, so layoffs remain low.

risk_factors: September payroll growth has tended to underperform its recent trend when Labor Day falls late in the month, as it did this year.

August's payroll strength came from outsized local education and leisure and hospitality gains that may not repeat, and poor seasonal adjustment in those series adds volatility to the monthly readings.
Survey-based employment signals have been less reliable post-pandemic, so strength in the survey trackers may not carry into payrolls.

tension_points.bull_case: Layoffs remain low, with jobless claims at 204k, the JOLTS layoff rate at 1.0% and Challenger layoffs at 52k. Alternative data averaged +77k versus +31k in August.
tension_points.bear_case: A late Labor Day has historically coincided with payroll underperformance versus trend, and August's 104k of education and leisure gains are not expected to repeat.

theme_stances.key_argument: Low layoffs and stronger alternative data are offset by a late Labor Day and non-repeating August gains, leaving payrolls slightly below consensus.
theme_stances.evidence: payroll growth has generally underperformed the recent trend
